 Rob and Michele Reiner’s daughter quietly sold house across from parents’ death home for $10.3 million — new owner takes staggering tax hit 
 By 
 Nate Grant and 
 Lucas Widman 
 Published 
 Nov. 18, 2026, 5:19 p.m. ET 
 See more of our coverage in your search results. 
 Make Page Six a Preferred Source 
 Romy Reiner, the daughter of the late Rob and Michele Reiner, quietly sold her home for $10.3 million.
 The property sat across the street from where her parents were found murdered, and the new owner is now facing a staggering $469,708 tax and recording-fee bill. The property was purchased by Hanochad, LLC, according to real estate records, with the sale recorded Feb. 17.
 The new owner was hit with $11,330 in documentary transfer taxes and $458,350 in City of Los Angeles transfer taxes, along with $28 in recording fees.

 The three-bedroom, three-bathroom farmhouse, which had been owned by the Reiner family for over 30 years, sits directly across from the Reiners’ primary residence—where the famed filmmaker and his wife were slain last year. 
 The home features a tennis court and sits on a nearly half-acre-sized lot.
 Page Six can confirm that the home was purchased by a doctor affiliated with UCLA, who declined to comment on the purchase.

 Romy, 28, had been living at the home before her parents were found dead in their residence in December. 
 Rob and Michele were found with wounds consistent with knife injuries , and the case sent shockwaves through Hollywood. 
 Her brother, Nick Reiner, 33, has since been charged with their murders. Nick has pleaded not guilty to the murders following his Dec. 14 arrest.

 Nick was seen in court last month glaring at prosecutors during a hearing centered around whether the grand jury transcripts and exhibits that led to his indictment should be made public. 
 Weeks later, during a continuation of the hearing, Nick appeared anxious in court and on edge while looking directly at his lawyer and the judge. 
 Also in October, an attorney for the trust’s successor trustee, Jodi Pais Montgomery, asked a judge to approve a $300 payment from Nick’s trust to his jail commissary account, describing the request as a modest expense necessary for his “quality of life” behind bars.
